original_question: Consider a compact planar body B with piecewise smooth boundary and uniformly distributed mass moving in Newtonian aerodynamics through a medium of initially stationary point particles that reflect elastically from the body. When B has a simple shape such as an ellipse, a triangle, or the rod [-1,1] x {0}, what is the resulting motion of B for t >= 0, allowing translation and rotation?
target_in_paper: Alexander Plakhov’s open problem titled "motion in Newtonian aerodynamics" (the problem on journal p. 417 asking to describe the motion of a simple planar body such as an ellipse, triangle, or rod under Newtonian-aerodynamics collisions with resting particles). The immediately following problem, "equations of motion in a rarefied medium," is nearby context but is a separate problem, not the main target of your draft. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper on the core ingredients: a planar body B with piecewise smooth boundary and uniformly distributed mass, interaction with an initially stationary medium of point particles via elastic reflection, the representative simple shapes (ellipse, triangle, rod [-1,1] x {0}), and the request to describe the body's translational/rotational motion for t >= 0. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
missing_details: The paper fixes the ambient space to R^2 and describes B as a solid body, i.e. a compact domain in R^2 with piecewise smooth boundary; the medium occupies the exterior of B. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
The total mass of the body is an explicit parameter m > 0. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

The medium is normalized to unit areal density: there are infinitely many zero-mass particles, and the total mass of particles contained in any domain D outside B equals area(D). ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

The reflection law is specified more precisely than just 'elastic reflection': if a particle hits a regular boundary point x, one passes to the inertial frame in which x is instantaneously at rest, and in that frame the usual billiard law applies. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

The statement is posed for motion beginning at t = 0; to make the question stand-alone, one should explicitly say that the initial translational and/or angular state is prescribed at t = 0. The paper says only that the body 'starts the (translational and/or rotational) motion.' ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
The trivial disc case is explicitly excluded. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

The official problem also includes special pure-rotation subquestions for the rod [-1,1] x {0}: whether the total number of turns is finite or infinite, whether the angular velocity tends to 0, and what its asymptotic behavior is as t -> +infinity. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

A second special case in the paper asks the same pure-rotation questions for centrally symmetric bodies such as an ellipse or a square, started about their center with no translation. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

Nearby context on the next page says that the body moves freely in the Newtonian-aerodynamics framework and asks for equations of motion plus existence/uniqueness; this helps explain the intended dynamical setting, but it is not the same problem as the one your draft is targeting. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
refined_question: In the planar Newtonian-aerodynamics model, let B be a solid body in R^2, i.e. a compact set with piecewise smooth boundary and uniformly distributed mass, of total mass m > 0. Outside B there is a uniform medium of initially resting point particles, normalized so that the total mass of particles in any exterior domain D equals area(D). When a particle hits a regular boundary point x of B, it is reflected elastically according to the usual billiard law in the inertial frame in which x is instantaneously at rest. If at time t = 0 the body begins a prescribed translational and/or rotational motion, describe the subsequent motion of B for all t >= 0 when B has a simple nontrivial shape such as an ellipse, a triangle, or the rod B = [-1,1] x {0}, excluding the disc. In particular, if the rod, or more generally a centrally symmetric body such as an ellipse or square, starts in pure rotation about its center with no translation, is the total number of turns finite or infinite, does the angular velocity tend to 0 as t -> +infinity, and what is its asymptotic behavior? ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
justification: The draft is a very close paraphrase of Alexander Plakhov’s problem "motion in Newtonian aerodynamics": the same R^2 setting, the same uniformly distributed body in a medium of initially resting particles, the same elastic-collision rule, the same sample shapes, and the same request to describe the motion for t >= 0. The only paper-faithful additions needed to make it fully stand-alone are the density normalization of the medium, the precise local reflection law, the explicit exclusion of the disc, and the pure-rotation subquestions for the rod and centrally symmetric bodies. The next-page problem on equations of motion/existence-uniqueness is explicitly marked as closely connected, so it supplies context about the intended dynamical framework, but it should not replace the actual target problem. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
